statements.text: I am Chair of the Subcommittee on Emerging Threats (ETSO), a Subcommittee of this Homeland Security Committee, and I focus there, among other things, on the risks that artificial intelligence could pose to the cybersecurity of critical infrastructure like electric grids and hospitals. [...] can you expand a little bit, how does AI impact the cybersecurity threat landscape and are there opportunities to utilize AI to counter these threats?
statements.context: Senate Homeland Security Committee hearing on AI risks and opportunities, where the senator chairs the Subcommittee on Emerging Threats.

statements.text: And to Mr. Barrans, through emerging artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, bad actors are increasingly able to rapidly produce realistic scam emails that can target VA beneficiaries, along with lots of other people, but we are focused on VA here.
statements.context: Senate hearing on protecting veterans from financial exploitation, questioning a VA official.

statements.text: Well, one of the things we are seeing, for instance, is AI-enabled scams through the IRS, or pretending to be the IRS.
statements.context: Remarks during a Senate hearing on preventing financial exploitation of veterans and their benefits.

statements.text: AI researchers have highlighted some of the potential public safety risks posed by AI systems. These safety concerns include AI systems providing dangerous information to bad actors or potentially acting in unpredictable ways that run counter to the intent of designers.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in Government, Senator Hassan posing a question to a witness panel.

statements.text: I do have another question for you, Dr. Parker, on deep fakes, which are obviously images and videos that are generated artificially, and they are becoming increasingly realistic. [...] As artificial intelligence advances, deep fakes like the Zelensky one will become harder to identify and debunk, and I am concerned that in the hands of our adversaries, deep fakes pose a really significant threat.
statements.context: Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence in Government, Senator Hassan questioning a witness.

statements.text: Congress created the National AI Initiative Office to improve efficiency and help Federal and local governments, researchers, business leaders, and other stakeholders collaborate on AI issues. You were the first National AI Director, but that position has remained vacant since you left the post in August. As the former Director, why is it important that we fill this position?
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in government, Senator Hassan questioning a witness about the vacant National AI Director position.

statements.text: However, the strategy does not currently require a strategic level focus on safeguards to prevent AI from being used in a manner that harms our country or society.
statements.context: Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence in Government, where Senator Hassan questions an expert witness on integrating safeguards into the national AI strategy.

statements.text: Now, I understand AI is a little bit different, but could a FedRAMP type program, or an entity with aspects that FedRAMP has, that is designed to specifically evaluate AI products be a feasible option for evaluating the safety of those AI products?
statements.context: Senate hearing on governing AI through federal acquisition and procurement.

statements.text: I am concerned about potential public safety and national security ramifications of AI. Dr. Li, you have raised concerns about AI behaving in unintended or unpredictable ways that could be detrimental to Americans. What are the key considerations for Federal acquisition and procurement policy to ensure the safety of AI?
statements.context: Senate hearing on governing AI through acquisition and procurement, during a round of questions chaired by Senator Hassan.

statements.text: I helped lead a bipartisan effort to codify the General Service Administration's IT Modernization Centers of Excellence, including the Center of Excellence for Artificial Intelligence. [...] In your view, is the AI Center of Excellence equipped to provide support to all agencies, especially smaller agencies seeking to procure and adopt AI? If not, how could it be improved?
statements.context: Senate hearing on governing AI through acquisition and procurement, with a senator questioning a witness on GSA support for federal AI adoption.

statements.text: I am concerned that Federal efforts to adopt and use AI may not be successful if we continue to rely on legacy IT. Could the Federal Government's aging infrastructure prevent us from effectively adopting AI technology?
statements.context: Senate hearing on governing AI through federal acquisition and procurement.

statements.text: Can you comment on the risk posed by bad actors who could use AI to develop drug analogs that could potentially skirt existing laws and interdiction efforts?
statements.context: Senate hearing on advanced technology and national-security threats, Senator Hassan questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: At last week's AI forum here in the Senate, an AI researcher told Senators that his team was able to get Meta's AI system to provide instructions for how to develop a biological weapon. According to the researcher, all it took was $800 and a few hours of work. This is an example of a jailbreak which bad actors such as terrorists can use to evade the safeguards in AI systems. Is there risk of bad actors using AI to develop modified biological or chemical weapons?
statements.context: Senate hearing on advanced technology and national security threats, where Senator Hassan questions an expert witness about AI-enabled CBRN risks.

statements.text: Dr. Murdick, I want to take a moment to consider some of the very serious risks posed by artificial intelligence. [...] To comprehensively address these kinds of risks in the long run, we have to strive to make AI fundamentally safe, meaning it cannot easily be abused by criminals and cannot easily behave in unexpected ways that harm the public.
statements.context: Senate hearing on advanced technology and national security threats, where Senator Hassan questions an expert witness on AI safety research.

statements.text: For example, although there has been considerable congressional attention paid to many of the public safety risks posed by artificial intelligence, there has been less focus on so-called catastrophic risks posed by AI, such as the ability of AI to help terrorists develop and use unconventional weapons. [...] I am working on a framework to support research into safer AI that, in its fundamental design, cannot easily be abused by criminals and cannot easily behave in unexpected ways that would harm the public.
statements.context: Opening statement by Senator Hassan at a Senate Subcommittee hearing on advanced technology threats to national security, also serving as a farewell to retiring Ranking Member Romney.

statements.text: As we develop powerful artificial intelligence and it becomes even more integrated into our daily lives, I think there need to be safeguards that protect the lives of Americans. [...] develop AI that is fundamentally safer and either cannot be exploited or at least is much harder to exploit for dangerous uses?
statements.context: Senate hearing on advanced technology and national security threats, with the senator questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: In the spring, the Biden Administration announced new controls to prevent the exportation of certain advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. This is an important step that will hopefully slow down Chinese development of the types of chips needed to produce powerful artificial intelligence systems.
statements.context: Senate hearing on advanced technology and national security threats, where Senator Hassan questions a witness about semiconductor export controls and multilateral coordination.

statements.text: Just last week, the Committee heard from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Christopher Wray, that the most persistent terrorist threats to the United States are small groups or lone actors who sometimes commit acts of violence after watching or reading online content that glorifies extreme or hateful views. [...] Professor, what lessons can we learn from history about how major technology advancements can contribute to a climate of extremism, and what recommendations do you have for Congress to mitigate how AI systems may contribute to extremism in the United States?
statements.context: Senator Hassan poses a question to a professor at a hearing examining the societal impact of AI through a historical lens.

statements.text: Well then—as a follow-up, how can Congress help support the use of AI to better predict and combat AMR?
statements.context: Senator Hassan asks a follow-up question during a Senate hearing on AI in health care about congressional support for AI applications combating antimicrobial resistance.

statements.text: Artificial intelligence can be helpful when designing new tools to combat the threat of antimicrobial resistance. For example, researchers at the NIH have found that machine learning algorithms can quickly analyze patterns in antimicrobial resistance. This can obviously help public health authorities respond to outbreaks of resistant infections more quickly and efficiently. Artificial intelligence also has the potential to help doctors more precisely diagnose and treat an infection with the right antibiotic at the right dose.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in health care where Senator Hassan questions a witness about AI applications in combating antimicrobial resistance.

statements.text: I am particularly concerned about Chinese AI tools that are used for surveillance and censorship, and how these tools may undermine democracy and freedom around the world.
statements.context: Senator Hassan questions a witness during a Senate hearing on AI's philosophical and societal implications.

statements.text: Algorithms can help physicians categorize and structure patient data, making it easier for health care providers to access and use. [...] we need standards in AI for medical settings in order to ensure that patients are receiving the best possible care and that their privacy is protected. [...] How can Congress support the development and implementation of these kinds of standards?
statements.context: Senator Hassan asks a witness during a Senate hearing on AI in health care about congressional action to develop AI standards for medical settings.

statements.text: Your testimony discusses the possibility that bad actors can use AI in ways that threaten national security, such as in the bioengineering and nuclear fields. What would you recommend Congress do to minimize national security risks posed by the misuse of AI?
statements.context: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on AI philosophy and policy, November 8, 2023.

statements.text: Thank you, Mr. Chair. thank you to our witnesses for being here, not only for your testimony, but for the work that you do. My questions are really going to be follow-ons or expansions of, I think, the questions you have heard, because there is a common focus among all of us about how we can maximize the potential of AI, but also protect the things that people care about in their interactions with government in the process.
statements.context: Senator Hassan poses questions during a Senate hearing on using AI to improve federal government services and customer experience.

statements.text: However, we cannot use AI to make these connections without adequate data-sharing policies or data-sharing infrastructure.
statements.context: Senate hearing on using AI to improve government services and customer experience.

statements.text: what are some of the ways that AI could supplement or complement the work of Federal customer service representatives so that they can focus on the people who actually need the human one-on-one case management or solving?
statements.context: Senate hearing on using AI to improve government services and customer experience, where Senator Hassan questions an expert panel.

statements.text: Mr. Kurland, earlier you mentioned that BIS would be adding six new entities to your agency list because they were providing AI tech to China. Can you tell the Subcommittee more about their efforts to undermine export controls?
statements.context: Senate Subcommittee hearing on improving export controls enforcement, Senator Hassan questioning a witness about BIS entity-list additions.

statements.text: last year I led a bipartisan push with Senators Wyden, Grassley, and Lankford for the IRS to address possible tax scams fueled by artificial intelligence. One concern that we raised is that scammers can target seniors and small businesses with convincing AI-generated emails that claim to be from the IRS.
statements.context: Senate Finance Committee hearing on the IRS FY2025 budget and 2024 filing season, featuring exchange between Senator Hassan and IRS Commissioner Danny Werfel.

statements.text: As artificial intelligence (AI) improves so does the ability of criminals to deceive and defraud Americans. With this new technology, criminals can impersonate loved ones, develop advanced malware, or make more convincing phishing messages.
statements.context: Senate hearing on DHS's FY2026 budget request, Senator Hassan questioning Secretary Noem.

statements.text: Mr. Allende, under the 2024 DHS artificial intelligence (AI) Roadmap, the Science and Technology (S&T) Directorate is set to build out the infrastructure needed to evaluate the risk that terrorists and criminals could misuse powerful AI models, right? [...] they classified as having a high capability of producing biological harm, including dangerous pathogens.
statements.context: Senate hearing on nominations including Pedro Allende, where Senator Hassan questions the nominee for Under Secretary of Science and Technology about AI risk prioritization.

statements.text: You must have some experience then in prioritizing what kind of risks you are looking at? My question, this is urgent. I mean, this is a national security and public safety matter, and it is an urgent one. We have open AI saying they have now got an AI that is highly capable of producing biological harm. This is on our doorstep. It's a national security issue. Do you feel urgency about it? What's your plan to make sure that you are focused on the most serious threats?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for nominees, where Senator Hassan presses a nominee on prioritizing AI biosecurity threats.

statements.text: By Ms. HASSAN (for herself and Mr. Banks): S. 3336. A bill to require the Secretary of Homeland Security to carry out prize competitions to advance the science of interpretability and to develop adversarial robustness with respect to artificial intelligence products [...]
statements.context: Senate floor introduction of bills and joint resolutions, where Senator Hassan introduced S. 3336 by title.
